text:
**Short answer: about 200–300 W of solar panels will recharge a 1,000 Wh power station in roughly 1 to 1.5 days of decent sun. For a full recharge in a single day, plan on about 300 W (summer) or more.**

**The math**

Daily energy ≈ panel watts × peak sun hours × ~0.7–0.75 (real-world losses from heat, angle, and charge controller).

- **200 W panel:** about 600–630 Wh/day at 4–4.5 peak sun hours, so roughly 1.5 days to refill from empty ([Watt48](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station), [Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).
- **Full recharge in one day** (watts needed ≈ 1,000 ÷ (sun hours × 0.75)), from [Power Runtime](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/):
  - 3 sun hours: ~450 W
  - 4 sun hours: ~340 W
  - 5 sun hours: ~270 W
  - 6 sun hours: ~230 W
- A quick rule of thumb: battery Wh ÷ 5 gives the panel wattage that refills it in about a day and a half ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).

**Things that change the answer**

- **Season and location:** Most of the US averages 3–6 peak sun hours. In a northern winter (about 2 hours), a one-day refill can take 700 W or more ([Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)).
- **Your station's solar input limit:** Many 1,000 Wh units cap solar input anywhere from 200 W to 800 W. Panels beyond the cap add nothing, so check your model's spec sheet.
- **Voltage:** The panels' open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay within your station's input window. Exceeding it can damage the charge controller, and wiring panels in series adds voltage. Parallel is generally the safer choice.
- **Using power while charging:** Net charging is solar input minus your load, so recharging will be slower if you're running devices.

**A practical pick**

If your station accepts 400 W or more of input, the ALLPOWERS SP037 400 W foldable panel would refill 1,000 Wh in about a day in good sun. It lists a Voc of 45.3 V, which fits 12–60 V solar inputs, and MC4→XT60 and DC adapters are included. It's $299 (about $269.10 with code ALLPOWERS26, which the retailer site says expires 2026-12-30). Note that it weighs 18.5 kg (about 41 lb), and it's too high-voltage for stations with a low input window, such as 5–24 V or 12–28 V models. [Buy it here](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-sp037-400w-solar-panel) (affiliate link; details at [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/allpowers-sp037-400w-solar-panel)).

If your station caps at 200 W, a 200 W panel is the right size, and it will take about a day and a half. Tell me which power station you have and I can check what it accepts and suggest a matching panel.
